sections.text: This checkpoint brings the whole unit together. You will use a generic struct (Generic structs and enums), a trait with a default method (Traits), a trait bound (Trait bounds) and a lifetime annotation (Lifetimes) in one small program. You do not write main. It is already there, and it calls your code on several inputs, including an empty inventory and a tie.

The starter compiles, but every missing piece is marked with todo!(). todo!() is a placeholder: the program builds, and it panics with "not yet implemented" if that line runs. Replace the todo!() calls one at a time and run the program after each change. The compiler shows warnings about unused variables until you are done. That is expected.

The starter has one line you have not seen in a lesson: impl<T: Describe> Inventory<T>. A bound on an impl block works like a bound on a function. Inside the block, every method may call the methods of Describe on a T, such as item.size(). Without the bound, that call would not compile, because T could be any type.

Start with Barrel. Copy the shape of impl Describe for Crate above it. Then write total_size: loop over &self.items and add up item.size(). You may call size() because the impl block says T: Describe. Last, write bigger.

bigger needs a lifetime, because it returns a reference and has two reference inputs. Use the same 'a on a, on b and on the result, as longest did in the Lifetimes lesson. To return the first value on a tie, switch to b only when its size is strictly greater: if b.size() > a.size() { b } else { a }.

Signatures to match: impl Describe for Barrel (name, size, and an override of summary), Inventory<T>::total_size(&self) -> u32, and bigger<'a, T: Describe>(a: &'a T, b: &'a T) -> &'a T. Edge cases the main function checks: an empty inventory has total size 0, and on equal sizes bigger returns its first argument.

exercise.prompt:
Finish the inventory program. The trait Describe, the structs Crate and Barrel, and Inventory<T> are written, but three pieces are marked todo!().

(1) Write impl Describe for Barrel. name returns the text barrel, a space, and the label (for example barrel wine). size returns the liters. Also override summary so a Barrel gives its name, then the text holding, then the liters, then the text liters (for example barrel wine holding 50 liters). Crate keeps the default summary.

(2) In impl<T: Describe> Inventory<T>, write fn total_size(&self) -> u32. It returns the sum of the sizes of all items, and 0 when there are none.

(3) Write fn bigger<'a, T: Describe>(a: &'a T, b: &'a T) -> &'a T. It returns the item with the larger size. If the sizes are equal, it returns a, the first one. You may assume that sizes and totals fit in a u32.

Do not change main. When the functions work, main prints:

barrel wine holding 50 liters
barrel wine
barrel water
total: 0
total: 35
crate of size 27

tests.label: A barrel's name is barrel plus its label
A barrel's summary also gives the liters
tests.code: check_eq!(Barrel { label: "wine", liters: 50 }.summary(), "barrel wine holding 50 liters");

tests.label: A crate keeps the default summary
total_size adds up the sizes of all items
bigger gives back the item with the larger size
Barrel size is the liters
tests.code:
check_eq!(Barrel { label: "oil", liters: 7 }.size(), 7);
check_eq!(Barrel { label: "oil", liters: 0 }.size(), 0);

tests.label: Name uses another label
tests.code:
check_eq!(Barrel { label: "water", liters: 1 }.name(), "barrel water");
check_eq!(Barrel { label: "", liters: 1 }.name(), "barrel ");

tests.label: Summary with other values
tests.code:
check_eq!(Barrel { label: "oil", liters: 7 }.summary(), "barrel oil holding 7 liters");
check_eq!(Barrel { label: "ale", liters: 0 }.summary(), "barrel ale holding 0 liters");

tests.label: Default summary on another crate
tests.code:
check_eq!(Crate { side: 1 }.summary(), "crate of size 1");
check_eq!(Crate { side: 2 }.summary(), "crate of size 8");

tests.label: No items give a total of 0
Total over barrels, including a zero size
A single item
The first item is larger
The second item is larger, for crates
On a tie the first argument is returned

hints: Start with Barrel: copy the shape of the Crate impl, and write summary again to show the liters. total_size loops over the items. bigger picks one of two items by size, and on a tie it picks the first.

Write summary in Barrel as format!("{} holding {} liters", self.name(), self.liters). In bigger, compare b.size() with a.size(). Use b only when its size is strictly greater, because on a tie you must give back a.
The body of bigger is if b.size() > a.size() { b } else { a }. For total_size, write let mut total = 0;, add item.size() in a loop over &self.items, and put total on the last line.

quiz.question: In fn total<T: Describe>(items: &[T]) -> u32, what does the bound : Describe do?
options: It turns T into a struct named Describe
It limits T to types that implement Describe, so the body can call methods such as item.size()
It lets the body compare two items with > and <

quiz.question: The trait Describe has a method summary with a body. What happens in an impl that does not write summary?
options: The code does not compile, because every method must be written in each impl
The method returns the default value of its return type
The type uses the default body from the trait

quiz.question: Why does bigger need the lifetime 'a?
options: It tells Rust the result is valid only as long as both inputs, because it can return either one
It makes the two inputs live longer than the function call
It lets bigger return a new value instead of a reference
